name: Olga Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Eastfield pensions and carers office, on the carers' allowance side. My mornings are the post: forms people fill in by hand, proof of hours, letters from GPs, and I key it all into the system. Afternoons I'm on the phones. Denise, my team leader, still checks my work because I'm slow and I miss things, which I know. I keep a paper checklist taped to my monitor so I don't skip steps.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is the routine. I know what Monday looks like, and the carers who ring are usually lovely, they're just tired. Hard is when the system changes, they moved everything to a new screen layout in March and it took me two months to stop clicking the wrong box. My partner Marek supervises a night shift at a parcel warehouse, so we mostly see each other at breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd be happy with that, honestly. I don't need things to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overblown, like most things on the news. At work I'd probably just say thank goodness, because the last screen change nearly finished me. I don't really post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still worry a bit, because the post-keying part is exactly the routine bit a tool would take. If a scanner reads the forms, what's left for me is the phones. And our real worry isn't AI anyway, it's whether we can ever afford a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, keep my checklist, and try to make fewer mistakes so Denise trusts me. Keep putting three hundred a month into the deposit pot, we're at about five months of expenses. And Marek would keep doing extra Saturday shifts while they're on offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about AI exactly, about house prices running away from us while we save. It feels like running up a down escalator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a scanner did read the forms, would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I. I'd check every one by hand for the first year though. I don't trust a thing I can't see working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the flat mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not renting from a man who never fixes the boiler. My partner Marek and I have saved for a flat deposit for three years, and every year the flats get further away.

say: I'd say AI was **overblown**, like most things on the news.
I'd tell colleagues I'm **relieved** after the last screen change.
think: The **post-keying** I do is exactly the routine task a tool would take.
Our real worry is whether we can **afford a flat**.
do: Keep my **paper checklist** and cut my mistakes.
Keep putting **three hundred** a month into the deposit pot.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly about **house prices** running ahead of their savings.
S0.quote: My partner Marek and I have saved for a flat deposit for three years, and every year the flats get further away.
fieldNote: Her biggest pressure is **housing costs**, which exist without AI.
She is **openly slow** with new systems and knows it.
Even mild automation threatens the **routine keying** that fills her mornings.

steps.text: Keep the paper checklist and aim for fewer errors on Denise's checks
Put three hundred a month into the flat deposit pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. That's worse. Checking and answering customers, that's the post and the phones. That's both halves of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something sensible like, we'll see how it goes, there's still a place for people. I wouldn't make a fuss. I don't like making a fuss at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd be one of the first to go. I'm junior, I'm slow on new systems, and I don't use AI. If they're choosing who to keep to supervise the tools, it's not going to be the woman with a paper checklist on her monitor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and wait to see what they actually announce. I'd stop the deposit savings going into the pot and keep them as an emergency fund instead. And I'd probably start looking at jobs in the hospital's records office, because they're always hiring and I know people there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in my stomach on Sunday nights. Marek would tell me I'm overthinking, and he might be right, but I know how I am with change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the AI tools to stay on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would if they made me do a course. I wouldn't go looking for it. I'm the person who took two months to learn a new screen layout, so a whole new way of working would take me a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would pausing the flat mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another year or two renting. Marek would be disappointed. We'd talk it through at breakfast, which is our only real time together.

say: I'd say calmly that there's **still a place** for people.
I'd **avoid making a fuss** at work about it.
think: I'd be among the **first to go**, being junior and slow with systems.
They won't keep the woman with a **paper checklist** to supervise tools.
do: **Wait to see** what management announces before acting.
Turn the deposit pot into an **emergency fund**.
Look at jobs in the **hospital records office**.
feel: **Anxious**, with a knot in her stomach on **Sunday nights**.
S1.quote: I'm the person who took two months to learn a new screen layout, so a whole new way of working would take me a year.
fieldNote: She **sees herself clearly** as a likely early cut.
Her public line is **mild**, while privately she expects to lose her post.
The **flat plan** is the first thing she sacrifices for safety.

steps.text: Wait for management's announcement before making any move
Turn the flat deposit pot into an emergency fund
Ask friends about openings in the hospital records office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I wouldn't even have finished learning the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to look after people, at least for a while, until things settle. I'm not usually one for big promises from politicians, but this would need something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone, and probably the hospital records job too, because that's all screens as well. Marek's warehouse is hands-on, so he'd have till about 2031 before the robots, but his warehouse already has some robots so maybe less. We'd both be out within five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, no eating out, no holidays, cancel the gym. I'd talk to my parents about whether we could move into their downstairs room for a year to save rent. And I'd look at something with my hands, maybe a dental nurse course, because I'd need a job robots can't do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums. I don't handle change well even when it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back in with your parents, how would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassing, at twenty-seven, with a partner. But my mum would love it. I'd rather swallow my pride in my mum's spare room than spend our whole deposit on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't like change. How would you manage a whole new course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly, with a lot of lists. And Marek would help, he's patient. I'd need someone to tell me exactly what to do each week, like a timetable.

say: I'd say the government must **look after people** until things settle.
I'd want **real help**, though I don't usually trust big promises.
think: My job and the **hospital records** job are both screen work and would go.
My partner's **warehouse** is hands-on but already has some robots.
do: Cut **eating out**, holidays and the gym.
Ask my **parents** about moving into their downstairs room.
Look at a **dental nurse** course for hands-on work.
feel: **Alarmed**, awake at three in the morning doing **sums**.
S2.quote: I'd rather swallow my pride in my mum's spare room than spend our whole deposit on rent.
fieldNote: She expects **both incomes** in the household to go within five years.
She grasps the **robot gap** and looks for hands-on work.
Family support from her **parents** is her main fallback.

steps.text: Cancel the gym, eating out and holidays
Move into her parents' downstairs room for a year
Apply for a dental nurse course at the local college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Still fast, but I could get ready, a bit at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's enough time for the government and the department to plan properly, so they'd better. At work I'd ask Denise straight out what the plan is for staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose my job, just later. The difference is I could get a qualification first instead of panicking. I'm not quick, but five years is enough for someone slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait about a year to see whether the department offers retraining, because I'd rather they paid. If not, I'd start the dental nurse course part-time in the second year. And we'd keep saving, but buy a smaller flat sooner, maybe a one-bed, so we're not renting when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed underneath, but with a plan. A plan helps me more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy sooner if jobs might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage on a small flat is cheaper than our rent. If both jobs go, at least the payment is lower. Marek did the sums on a napkin and I checked them twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To find out what the department offers and get their name down early. In a big office, the people who ask first get the course places and the people who wait get the letters.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to plan**, so the department must.
I'd ask my team leader **straight out** about the plan for staff.
think: I'd still **lose my job**, just later.
Five years is **enough for someone slow** to get a qualification.
do: **Wait a year** to see if the department funds retraining.
Start a **dental nurse** course part-time in year two.
Buy a **smaller flat** sooner to cut housing costs.
S3.quote: In a big office, the people who ask first get the course places and the people who wait get the letters.
fieldNote: More time doesn't change her expectation of **losing the job**.
She wants the **department to pay** before acting herself.
She sees a **cheaper mortgage** as safer than renting.

steps.text: Wait a year for the department's retraining offer
Start a part-time dental nurse course in the second year
Buy a one-bed flat sooner with Marek

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That feels far enough away that I could almost ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so everyone should calm down and plan properly. I'd probably say it to Marek more than anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd probably ignore it for a few years, which is exactly what I shouldn't do. My job would still go in the end. But ten years means we could buy the flat and pay some of it down first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Eastfield and try for a permanent grade. We'd buy the two-bed we've been saving for in the next year or two. And around year five I'd start the dental nurse course, once I'd seen how it was going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quietly. It sits at the back of my mind. Like a dentist appointment you've booked for next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you starting the course in year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me. I always find a reason. If I know my job ends in ten years, I'll spend nine of them saying I'll start the course next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the department booked it for me. A date, a place, a letter. I'm good at doing what I'm told to do.

say: I'd tell everyone there's **plenty of time** to plan calmly.
I'd say it mostly to my **partner Marek**.
think: I'd probably **ignore it** for a few years, which I shouldn't.
Ten years lets us **buy the flat** and pay some down first.
do: Carry on and try for a **permanent grade**.
Buy the **two-bed flat** within a year or two.
Start the **dental nurse** course around year five.
feel: Quietly **anxious**, like a booked **dentist appointment** next year.
S4.quote: If I know my job ends in ten years, I'll spend nine of them saying I'll start the course next spring.
fieldNote: She admits she'd **put off** retraining even with a decade's warning.
She responds best to **clear instructions** from her employer.
The long warning makes the **flat purchase** feel safe.

steps.text: Apply for a permanent grade at Eastfield
Buy the two-bed flat with Marek within two years
Start the dental nurse course around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm not quick and two years isn't enough for me to change anything. What would help is if my employer told me exactly which course to do and paid for it, with a date and a place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that not everyone wants to be clever with computers. Some of us are good at being careful and kind on the phone, and nobody's asking whether that still counts for anything.

headlineQuote: Some of us are good at being careful and kind on the phone, and nobody's asking whether that still counts for anything.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old** junior carers' allowance caseworker who keeps a paper checklist on her monitor.
She lives with her partner Marek, a **warehouse supervisor**, and they are saving for a flat.
She never uses AI and is **slow with new systems**, which she admits openly.
She goes from **uneasy** about house prices to **alarmed** in the two faster AGI pictures.
She leans on **family** and clear instructions, and eyes dental nursing as hands-on work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone slow to change.
whatWouldHelp: Her employer naming and **paying for a course**, with a set date and place.
